module_title: Dissolution of Firm, Unpaid Seller's Rights & Nemo Dat Rule
introduction: Tailored for advanced legal exams and UPSC Law Optional, this level explores the absolute dissolution of a partnership, the powerful equitable rights granted to an Unpaid Seller, and the strict rules (and exceptions) regarding the transfer of title by non-owners.

core_concepts.title: Dissolution of Partnership vs. Dissolution of Firm (Sec 39, IPA)
core_concepts.description:
A highly technical distinction:
- Dissolution of Partnership: Change in the relationship of the partners (e.g., admission, retirement, death of a partner). The firm/business continues to exist and operate.
- Dissolution of Firm: Complete breakdown of the relation among ALL partners. The business is wound up, assets are sold, and liabilities are paid off. 
- Court Dissolution (Sec 44): The court can dissolve a firm if a partner becomes of unsound mind, permanently incapable, guilty of conduct prejudicing the business, or if the business can only be carried on at a loss.

core_concepts.title: Rights of an Unpaid Seller (Section 45-54, SoGA)
core_concepts.description:
A seller is 'unpaid' if the whole price hasn't been paid, or if a cheque/bill of exchange was received but dishonored. They have three powerful rights against the goods:
1. Right of Lien (Sec 47): The right to retain possession of the goods until payment. This right depends strictly on **possession**. Once the seller hands the goods to a carrier/transporter, the lien is lost.
2. Right of Stoppage in Transit (Sec 50): If the buyer becomes **insolvent** AND the goods are still in transit (seller has lost possession, but buyer hasn't gained it yet), the seller can order the carrier to return the goods.
3. Right of Resale (Sec 54): If the goods are perishable, or if the seller gives notice to the buyer and the buyer still doesn't pay, the seller can resell the goods to a third party.

core_concepts.title: Nemo Dat Quod Non Habet (Section 27, SoGA)
core_concepts.description:
Meaning: 'No one can give what he does not have.'
- General Rule: If goods are sold by a person who is not the owner (and who doesn't have the owner's authority), the buyer acquires no better title to the goods than the seller had. (If a thief sells you a stolen watch, you do not become the legal owner).
- Exceptions: To protect bona fide commerce, the Act provides exceptions where a non-owner CAN pass good title:
  (1) Sale by a Mercantile Agent (Sec 27 proviso).
  (2) Sale by a joint owner in possession (Sec 28).
  (3) Sale by a person in possession under a voidable contract (before the contract is rescinded) (Sec 29).
  (4) Sale by an unpaid seller exercising their right of resale (Sec 54).

important_entities.name: Public Notice on Retirement (Section 32, IPA)
important_entities.key_fact: Liability continues until the world is informed.
important_entities.significance: When a partner retires, they MUST give a public notice of their retirement. If they fail to do so, they and the other partners continue to be mutually liable to third parties for any acts done by the firm after the retirement. The 'Holding Out' principle applies.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: The Lien vs. Stoppage in Transit Trap
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation:
Advanced exams often test the transition point between these two rights. 
- If the seller has the goods in his own godown -> **Lien**.
- If the seller gives the goods to a railway company to ship -> Lien ends. **Stoppage in transit** begins (but ONLY if the buyer is insolvent).
- If the buyer collects the goods from the railway station -> Stoppage in transit ends. The seller now only has a right to sue for the price (right against the person), and no rights against the goods.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Lien (Hold it), Stop (Catch it), Resale (Sell it)
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: The chronological escalation of an unpaid seller's rights depending on where the goods physically are.

exam_strategy_tips: In UPSC Mains, when discussing the exceptions to *Nemo dat quod non habet*, explicitly connect it to the doctrine of protecting the **'Bona Fide Purchaser for Value without Notice'** to show deep jurisprudential understanding.
